articles.summary: The Department of Transportation (DOTr) on Wednesday launched a bus augmentation program to mitigate the large volume of commuters using the LRT-2.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 1:50pm
The Department of Transportation (DOTr) on Wednesday launched a bus augmentation program to mitigate the large volume of commuters using the LRT-2.

A week after his return to the agency, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said that the LRT-2 could no longer serve 4,000 passengers during its peak hours. The number of passengers grew after the government implemented a 50% increase in train fares due to the Middle East fuel crisis.

“Sampung tren lang ang umaandar, ‘yun na 'yung maximum dahil 'yung mga ibang tren, dahil nga hindi na-maintain ng maayos, kulang sa pondo, all these years… 27, 25 years na 'yung tren, hindi na napalitan,” Dizon said in a media interview.

(There are only ten trains running; that is the maximum because the other trains were not maintained well due to lack of funding, all these years… the trains are 27, 25 years old and have not been replaced.)
“Talagang hindi kakayanin sa dami ng mga sumasakay na commuters dito sa linyang to,” he added.
(This line really could not handle the volume of commuters here.)

Dizon said that the bus augmentation program was an “out-of-the-box solution," as they could not get new trains yet. There will be 20 buses deployed beginning Wednesday, which will span from Antipolo to Cubao, with some reaching all the way to Legarda.
The regular fare is P80 from Antipolo to Legarda, but it will be P55 for students. The buses could accommodate up to 70 people if some of them are standing, according to Dizon.
The trial run is indefinite, but operations already started on Wednesday. The agency will also study applying the EDSA Busway format to Marcos Highway, Dizon added.
Dizon also said that plans to have a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) for the LRT-2 are still ongoing, but clarified that this does not mean that prices will increase.

“‘Pag sinabi natin PPP, hindi ibig sabihin no'n tataas ang pamasahe kasi ang control ng pasahe ay na sa gobyerno pa rin. Ang i-PPP natin 'yung operations and maintenance. At mas mabilis 'yung pag-procure at pag-maintain ng mga tren,” he said.

(When we say PPP, this does not mean that the fares will get higher because control over the fare is still with the government. We will let PPP handle the operations and maintenance. And the procurement and maintenance of trains will become faster.) —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Democrats aim to sweep most US governor elections after wins in key states
articles.summary: Party sees historic victories with Gina Hinojosa’s win in Texas and Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms becoming first Black female governor in US

blocks.text: Voters across the US have elected Democrats to lead many of the biggest states in the nation, marking a sea change in traditional Republican strongholds such as Georgia and Texas in what could have a profound effect on Donald Trump’s remaining term and the 2028 presidential election.

From Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia, making the former Atlanta mayor the first Black woman to be elected governor of any state, to Amy Acton’s win in reliably red Ohio, the results represented a repudiation of Trump, rank corruption in Washington and the power of billionaires to shape American politics. Democrats aimed to win a majority of governorships in the US, something they have not done since the 2006 midterm elections.

One of the biggest prizes of the night was the Texas governorship, with Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa unseating Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in a stunning upset. Hinojosa will be the first Latina governor of the state, and the first Democrat elected to the Texas governorship in 30 years.

Like Hinojosa’s win, considered unthinkable in the aftermath of Trump’s 2024 victory in Texas, Lance Bottoms’ win in Georgia against billionaire Rick Jackson also represented a stunning flip of a Republican stronghold, where the GOP has held the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislature for more than 20 years.

In Ohio, Democrat Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. The campaign drew national attention after Ramaswamy’s campaign aired a much-maligned ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, who lost custody of her children after her husband was accused of sexually abusing Acton as a child, sharply criticizing her daughter. Acton is the first Democrat elected governor in the state since 2006, and the first woman elected governor of Ohio.

Iowa Democrat Rob Sand pulled off an upset against Republican Zach Lahn, marking a major step towards the party rebuilding its standing in a state that has voted for Donald Trump three times and where the GOP has dominated state politics in recent years.

And in Wisconsin, Democrat David Crowley defeated Republican Tom Tiffany to become the state’s first Black governor. Crowley, who withdrew from the race only to rejoin at the urging of the outgoing Democratic governor, Tony Evers, overcame a massive fundraising gap to win the governorship.

Democrats also racked up gubernatorial victories in Pennsylvania, where popular incumbent Josh Shapiro handily defeated Stacy Garrity, and New York, where Kathy Hochul sailed to re-election. Democrat Deb Haaland was elected governor of New Mexico, making her the first Native American woman to win a governorship, while Xavier Becerra, also a Democrat, became California’s first elected Latino governor.
In Florida, Byron Donalds, Republican congressman and a strong Trump ally, edged out the former Republican turned Democrat David Jolly, becoming the Sunshine state’s first Black governor.

While media attention has focused intensely on the battle to control the US Congress, and whether Democrats could not only flip the House of Representatives but also win most of the Senate, upsets in gubernatorial races in traditionally Republican states could reset the map before the 2028 presidential contest.
Most of the so-called swing states that help determine who wins the White House – including Michigan and Wisconsin – are among the 36 states electing governors in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The first two years of Donald Trump’s second term as president have underscored the roles Democratic governors play in serving as a bulwark against Trump’s most excessive policies, including by filing lawsuits and other executive actions. While rules differ state by state, some governors appoint election officials who oversee elections, and can sign legislation to protect voter rights.
Republicans have held a majority of governorships since the 2010 election.

articles.title: James Talarico wins Texas Senate race in historic victory for Democrats
articles.summary: Jubilant Talarico says ‘Tonight we defeated Goliath’ as Ken Paxton defeat a crushing blow to Trump and Republicans

blocks.text: Democrat James Talarico has won the US Senate race in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold and delivering a stunning blow to Donald Trump.

Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and a staunch ally of the US president, in one of the most closely watched contests of the midterm elections to decide control of Congress.
“Tonight we defeated Goliath,” Talarico said to a jubilant crowd his election night party in Austin. “All the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas.”

The result has major implications for control of the Senate, where Republicans were defending a narrow majority, and complicate Trump’s efforts to advance his agenda during the final two years of his presidency.

The Democrat’s victory signifies a rupture in the political landscape in Texas, the country’s second biggest state, which Trump carried by nearly 14 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.
No Democrat had won a Senate seat in Texas since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988 and none had won any statewide office since 1994. Repeated attempts by the party to turn the state blue had fallen short.

A crowd erupted in cheers at Talarico’s watch party at a performing arts center in downtown Austin after the race was called. Supporters wearing Talarico T-shirts hugged one another and punched the air.

Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, said: “James Talarico just showed Democrats how to win in Texas by consistently challenging billionaire power, calling out Wall Street and Big Tech, and calling for bold structural change.”

Talarico, 37, will become the Senate’s youngest member and replace John Cornyn, 74, who lost a bruising Republican primary to the scandal-plagued Paxton, whose nomination bolstered Talarico’s appeal to Republican and independent voters.
Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, former middle school teacher and state representative, built his campaign around economic concerns, Christian faith and a message of political unity.

He sought to appeal to independents and Republicans disillusioned with the administration, arguing that the cost of living and the influence of wealthy donors mattered more to Texans than partisan divisions.

His campaign also sought to capitalise on controversies surrounding Paxton, 63, who, as attorney general, was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives in 2023 over allegations of corruption and abuse of power. He was acquitted by the state senate.
Separate securities fraud charges were resolved in 2024 under an agreement requiring community service, ethics training and restitution. Paxton denied wrongdoing.

The race became one of the most expensive Senate contests in US history, with advertising spending topping $500m, according to campaign spending estimates. Republican-aligned groups poured hundreds of millions of dollars into efforts to elect Paxton, including substantial funding linked to billionaire Elon Musk, whom Talarico accused of trying to buy a Senate seat.

“We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system, in this state, in this country, power belongs to the people,” Talarico said in his remarks on Tuesday night. “The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world and the entire DC establishment.”
Talarico countered the spending advantage with a formidable fundraising operation. His campaign reported raising $64m in the third quarter of the year, with 97% of donations under $100.

Republican advertising focused heavily on Talarico’s positions on transgender issues, his religious views, and his interpretation of scripture. Factcheckers have challenged claims made in some of the advertisements.

Trump rallied in Texas and branded him “James Talafreako” and falsely claimed that he is vegan, while Vice-President JD Vance implied that Talarico is gay, even though he has a girlfriend. Rightwing influencers even spread a false claim that he checked into a mental health clinic in Ohio (he was ill with flu).
Talarico portrayed Paxton as corrupt and argued that Republicans were attempting to distract voters from economic pressures, including rising fuel and everyday costs.

His victory represents a breakthrough for a party that had repeatedly come close to winning Texas in recent elections, only to fall short on polling day. Among those disappointments was the 2018 defeat of Beto O’Rourke by Ted Cruz by a margin of just under 215,000 votes, or 2.6%.
It is also a setback for Musk, who moved his personal residence to Texas and owns companies that are building datacenters there.

María Teresa Kumar, president and co-founder of Voto Latino, said: “For too long, Texas has been a state others wrote off. Voto Latino never did. We saw the energy building over the cycles, and we’ve always had faith in the state.

“Today, that demand for change turned into history. In a state where Latinos make up over 40% of the population, this win is proof that when young Latino voters are invested in and listened to, they flex their muscle and decide the future.”

articles.title: Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeats Texas governor Greg Abbott in stunning upset
articles.summary: Hinojosa wins momentous victory, shatters Republican grip on key office and will become state’s first Latina governor

blocks.text: In a stunning political upset that would have seemed improbable only a few weeks ago, Democrat Gina Hinojosa has defeated three-term governor Greg Abbott on Tuesday, shattering the Republican grip on the highest and most powerful executive office in Texas.

Hinojosa’s historic victory – she will be the state’s first ever Latina governor – ended Abbott’s bid for an unprecedented fourth term, and delivered Democrats their most consequential victory in the state in a generation.
“We shocked the world tonight,” Hinojosa told a crowd of cheering supporters after the race was called. “We showed that anything is possible.”

It was an extraordinary reversal of fortunes for Democrats in the Lone Star state, which has long frustrated the party’s hopes of a political comeback. A Democrat has not won the Texas governor’s mansion since 1990, when voters elected Ann Richards.

But since then, Democrats have struggled to convert a growing urban population and changing demographics into statewide victories. Even high-profile challenges, including by Beto O’Rourke who sought to unseat Abbott in 2022, ended in defeat.

Hinojosa, a five-term state representative from Austin, entered the governor’s race with little fanfare after other prominent Democrats declined to run against Abbott, a staunch ally of Donald Trump with a formidable fundraising operation and record of easily dispatching with his Democratic rivals.

At the outset, Hinojosa’s candidacy was viewed as the longest of long shots, overshadowed by the campaign of fellow Democrat James Talarico, which attracted considerably more national attention and enthusiasm. But Hinojosa gradually fought her way into contention, with some polls showing the race neck-in-neck.

“It never bothered me that they doubted me. It bothered me that they doubted us,” Hinojosa said in her victory speech. “Hundreds and millions on attack ads, written off over and over again. But Texas, my faith in you never wavered.”

She said Abbott had called to congratulate her and extended a “generous offer” to assist with the transition. “Now I stand before you, humbled and grateful, and in awe of the incredible grace and power of God and of Texas,” she added.

In his election night speech, Abbott announced to supporters that he had conceded, prompting a brief moment of stunned silence in the crowd. “You all helped me to be your governor for 12 years – thank you very much,” he said, adding that he was proud of making Texas the “headquarters of business headquarters”.
“Know that we are leaving Texas in far better shape than it’s ever been.”

A former Austin school board president, Hinojosa has said public education is the issue that drew her into the race, but her campaign widened to focus on affordability issues and her opposition to the expansion of large-scale data centers. Under Abbott, Texas has become a leading state in the nation for data center construction.
Abbott, who maintained a large financial advantage, sought to portray Hinojosa as too “woke” for Texas, attacking her in Trumpian terms as “gender-bender Hinojosa”.
Hinojosa countered the culture-war attacks on her with an ad declaring her pronouns: “Mom, Texan and soon-to-be governor”.
She sought to capitalize on growing frustration with Trump’s presidency, courting traditionally Republican constituencies with a populist economic message.

Hinojosa grew up along the US-Mexico border. Her mother is an immigrant from Mexico, and her father served for several years as the state Democratic party chair. Her sister, Xochitl Hinojosa, is a long-time Democratic operative who previously served as spokesperson for the Department of Justice.
Trump responded to the flurry of bad results on Tuesday night with a social media post on his Truth Social platform deflecting blame.
“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” said the president, who had repeatedly told his supporters to “pretend I’m on the ticket”.
The president then directly attacked Abbott, saying if he had not “become a RINO [Republican in name only] in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost”.
“He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!” Trump added, months after endorsing him as an “exceptional Governor and man”.

articles.title: Democrat Troy Jackson defeats Susan Collins to win Maine US Senate seat in blow to Republicans
articles.summary: Democratic nominee toppled the five-term Republican incumbent in one of the most hard-fought midterm contests

blocks.text: The Democrat Troy Jackson has won Maine’s US Senate race, toppling five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins in one of the biggest upsets of the 2026 midterms.

Jackson, 58, unseated Collins – who has been in the Senate since 1997 – in a closely fought, and often rancorous, race characterized by mutual accusations of corruption and clashes over living costs in the predominantly rural state.
The victory delivers Democrats one of their most coveted pickup opportunities this midterm cycle, and brings an end to Collins’ nearly three-decade tenure in Washington.

A lumberjack by trade and former state senate president, Jackson sought to break down Collins’ carefully crafted image as a moderate Republican willing to break with the Donald Trump, painting her instead as a loyal supporter of the president.

Jackson, who ran on a platform of progressive economic populism, had argued that Collins emboldened Trump’s agenda through critical votes, like confirming Brett Kavanaugh, the conservative supreme court justice – which paved the way for overturning the constitutional right to an abortion in the US.
Collins, meanwhile, cast Jackson as ideologically inconsistent and lacking the experience needed to deliver for Maine at the federal level.

As the only Senate Republican running in a state that Trump lost in 2024, Collins also argued that her independence and influence had delivered tangible results for Maine. She often pointed to the millions of federal dollars she had helped steer home as chair of the Senate appropriations committee.
Both of the nominees were courting a swathe of Mainers who were comfortable splitting the ticket in 2020 – voting for Joe Biden as president and sending Collins back to Washington for another term.

Maine has been hit hard by soaring fuel costs tied to Trump’s war with Iran and record-high heating oil prices, which began squeezing voters as temperatures fell in the weeks before the election. The state has also faced the pain of the administration’s sweeping tariffs, which have affected several of Maine’s most critical industries.
after newsletter promotion

The Senate saw a dramatic midterm cycle as the first Democratic nominee, Graham Platner, an oysterman and former marine, was forced to drop out amid a cascade of scandals that culminated in an allegation of sexual assault and rape, which he denied. Collins repeatedly sought to tie Jackson to Platner’s brand of progressivism, noting the two had campaigned together during Jackson’s unsuccessful gubernatorial bid earlier in the year.
Maine Democrats had just weeks to organize a special convention to select a replacement for Platner. After Jackson won, he had just 101 days to mount a Senate campaign.

articles.title: ERC issues show cause orders vs. 13 power firms over outages in Visayas, Mindanao
articles.summary: The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) has issued 24 show-cause orders (SCO) against 13 power generation companies over power outages that hit the Visayas and Mindanao.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 1:33pm
The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) has issued 24 show-cause orders (SCO) against 13 power generation companies over power outages that hit the Visayas and Mindanao.
The commission issued the SCOs on October 14 amid its ongoing assessment over concerns of frequent power supply interruptions and high electricity prices in the two islands.
The SCOs directed the firms to explain after 48 generating units were found to have exceeded the allowable Equivalent Unplanned Outage (EOU) limits, the ERC said.

"While the initial evaluation was completed to serve as the basis for these SCOs, the Commission has yet to receive the specific verified responses required under the newly issued Orders," the ERC said in a statement.

"Upon receipt of these subsequent submissions, the ERC will immediately evaluate the additional documents and supporting records to promptly resolve the cases in accordance with applicable rules and regulations," it added.

The ERC further warned that appropriate penalties shall also be imposed if concerned power generation companies found to have violated the prescribed reliability performance standards set by the commission.

"While underscoring the need to hold GenCos accountable for established violations, the ERC reiterated that all enforcement proceedings must observe due process and that any penalties imposed must be supported by evidence and grounded in applicable regulatory standards," the agency said.
Power outages have been frequent in the Visayas grid due to thin energy reserves.
To address this, the Department of Energy (DOE) earlier ordered the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) to install over 250 megawatts of battery energy storage system.
The DOE is also mulling to tap liquid fuel facilities to help provide additional power to the grid. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated
articles.summary: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find…

image.caption: From rotten food and sexual behavior to political beliefs, researchers want to know how different forms of disgust relate to our attitudesImage: picture alliance

blocks.text: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.
One explanation begins with evolution.
"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.
What are the three types of disgust?
But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

items: Pathogen disgust: Reactions to potential sources of infection, such as rotten food, vomit or bodily waste.
Sexual disgust: Reactions to particular sexual behaviors or situations.
Moral disgust: Reactions to wrongdoing, such as betrayal or cruelty. Researchers debate whether this reflects physical revulsion or moral disapproval.

blocks.text: One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump used language evoking contagion when describing immigrants early in his 2024 presidential campaignImage: Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.
"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."
Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.
"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.
Do liberals and conservatives feel disgust differently?
Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.
A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.
However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.
Can our bodies reveal our politics?
Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.
Many US voters are undecided, disillusioned or disengaged
But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.
Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.
"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.
How do gut feelings influence political beliefs?
Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.
"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."
The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."
They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.
But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.
What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

blocks.caption: Pathogen disgust is one type of disgust thought to have evolved to protect us from infectionImage: Elena Shishkina/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: "People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.
Can disgust actually be measured?
Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.
He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.
Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.
"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.
The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.
Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."
How might politicians exploit feelings of disgust?
Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.
"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.
Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?
"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.
Does disgust influence how people vote?

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.
"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.
Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.
"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."
Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.
He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.
"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said.

articles.title: UK apologises to Ukrainian child refugees who were told to study Russian
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Schools minister launches new Ukrainian GCSE and says she is sorry students were pushed to study Russian in its absence

The UK has apologised to Ukrainian child refugees who were…

blocks.text: The UK has apologised to Ukrainian child refugees who were told to study Russian in English schools, as it launched funding for a new GCSE in Ukrainian.

Ukrainian children who were forced to seek refuge in the UK after Vladimir Putin’s invasion in 2022 say it was “insulting” that their teachers suggested they study Russian in the absence of a GCSE in Ukrainian.

Announcing the new qualification, the schools minister, Georgia Gould, said: “So many students were pushed into having to do Russian. I’m really sorry that they were put in that position. It’s really important that they will have access to a Ukrainian GCSE.”
The new qualification, which will be ready in England in 2028, is being developed by the AQA exam board, with the help of a £340,000 grant from the Department for Education.

It comes after years of lobbying from the Ukrainian government and Ukrainian community groups on behalf of more than 30,000 Ukrainian children who have fled to the UK. In a letter to the DfE in 2024, the education ministry in Kyiv said: “We are deeply concerned that due to the lack of Ukrainian GCSE, many Ukrainian children are being pressured by their school staff to pass the Russian GCSE.”

Gould said: “It was one of the Ukrainian government’s asks of us that we deliver a Ukrainian GCSE, and one of the asks from the community and young people. We’re really proud to be able to do it, and proud of that partnership with the Ukrainian government.”
The Ukrainian language has been at the cultural frontline of the conflict with Russia. Putin has banned Ukrainian books and the teaching of Ukrainian in land Russia has occupied.
Gould said: “Whether it’s military support or this the kind of cultural support, our message as a British government is we stand absolutely steadfast behind the Ukrainian people.”

Ukraine’s education minister, Andrii Butenko, said he was grateful to the UK government. He said: “This will give Ukrainian children forced to leave their homes by Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine an equal opportunity to choose their native language as a GCSE subject. We will continue working with AQA and the DfE to develop a high-quality and accessible qualification.”

Gould made the announcement on a visit to St Mary’s school in west London, the centre of a network of 13 Ukrainian-language schools in the UK. She was introduced to Vitalii Andronik, 20, who told the Guardian in 2024 how he had been urged to study Russian GCSE as a 15-year-old refugee. Gould told him: “I’m really sorry that you were put in that position.”

Andronik welcomed the new qualification and the apology. He said: “It’s too late to me, but I want future generations of refugees to study Ukrainian. It’s a recognition of the trauma that we went through. It’s brilliant news to hear that in future kids here won’t have to study Russian.”

Sofiia Chonka, 16, who fled to London from Zakarpattia in south-west Ukraine in June 2024 with her family, said: “I was told to study Russia in year 9, I just said ‘no’. I didn’t want anything to do with Russia – they killed my people and injured my family.”

blocks.caption: Gould meets Ukrainian child refugees, including Sofiia Chonka on her left, who was told by teachers to study Russian but refused. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: Chonka, who has just started A-levels, said she would take the new exam when it was available. “It’s such a beautiful thing to be speaking Ukrainian when the Russians are trying to mute you.”
She added: “I’m really sad that it has taken so long, but at least they are starting the process, and some of my younger friends will have the opportunity to do it.
“It’s a stereotype that they are similar languages – they are completely different. Because Ukrainian is so beautiful, the Russians don’t like it. They can’t ban it, they can’t ban people.”

Inna Hryhorovych, the head of St Mary’s Trust, who has been calling for the GCSE since Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, said: “It’s still hard to comprehend that we don’t need to fight for this any more.” She said her next campaign would be a new A-level in Ukrainian.
Gould said: “We’re just doing GCSEs for now. Let’s see how it goes. But we really want this to be a success.”

The minister said exams board had been nervous about developing a new qualification for a relatively small cohort of students. She said: “Despite the challenges of a smaller qualification, we really wanted to put financial resources to making it possible, and I’m grateful that AQA has come forward.
“I want this to happen as quickly as possible for people, but I’m really glad that it is happening now. Some of the students sitting here today will be able to study this GCSE.”

She encouraged British children to study for the new qualification as an act of solidarity. “I think it would be wonderful if more people were taking up Ukrainian GCSE,” she said, and she joked that Ukrainian children could tutor their friends as a “side hustle”.
When Gould announced the plan to a dozen Ukrainian pupils, they applauded and in unison said “diakuyemo”, or “thank you very much”.

articles.title: US midterm election results: Democrats win crucial seats. Here's what else the data tells us
articles.summary: Democrats have won the majority in the US Senate. House of Representatives votes are still being counted. DW takes a look at who voted Republican, who voted Democrat and what it all means.

image.caption: In the midterms, Americans vote on whether Republicans or Democrats hold the majority in CongressImage: Datajournalism Midterms 2026

blocks.text: We will update this article throughout the night as more data becomes available, so keep checking back. DW follows the Associated Press (AP) for when a seat is called for Republicans or Democrats.

In the 2026 midterms, Americans voted on all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 members of the Senate. Before election night, Republicans held the majority in both Congress chambers, if only by a hair.

Midterm elections are held every four years. The results will influence US politics for the next few years. Despite the significant executive power delegated to the presidency according to the US Constitution, the majority of federal political decisions have to be approved by Congress before they can be implemented. If the Democrats win the majority in one or both chambers of Congress, it will be harder for President Donald Trump to govern as he chooses.
Live election results: Democrats win Senate majority
For ongoing updates, go to our US midterms live blog.

In the US Senate, Democrats have managed to flip six Republican seats, winning races in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Kansas, Texas and Iowa. With that, they have won the majority of 51 seats required to gain control of the chamber.

In the House of Representatives, all 435 seats are up for election. 218 seats are required to build a majority. Democrats have so far flipped 10 seats, for a total of 178 seats so far. Republicans have retained 106 seats.
How did Americans vote: a look at demographics and attitudes

The data on voter demographics and attitudes is based on a representative survey of more than 75,000 verified voters conducted by survey and market research firm SSRS on behalf of AP and other news organizations. It builds on interviews of both early and mail-in voters as well as exit polls of in-person voters on Election Day. Where percentages of Republican and Democratic voters don't add up to 100%, the remaining percent were voters who voted for third-party candidates.
Republicans lead among white men, Democrats among younger voters

Republicans continue to make up the majority of white male voters. 55% of white men polled voted Republican. On the opposite end of the spectrum are Black women, 91% of whom voted Democrat. Remarkably, the majority of both Latino men and women voted Democrat in this election. Two years ago, Latinos were a big part of the vote that carried Trump to his second term in the White House.
Age-wise, Democrats are strongest among young voters. Three-quarters of 18- to 24-year-olds voted Democrat. On the flipside, Republicans lead with 51% among voters aged 65 and up.
Latino voters turn away from Republicans

The data shows that Republicans have lost support among all demographic groups compared to the last midterms in November 2022. Even among white men, the share of those who voted Republican fell from 60% to 55%. Among white women, the Republicans' share fell from 56% to 48%, and among Latinos, the percentage of Republican voters decreased as well.
Democrats lead among urban voters and college graduates

The urban-rural divide that has been part of US politics for years continues to hold. Among urban voters, almost 70% voted Democrat, among suburban voters, that number stands at 57%. On the other hand almost 60% of rural and small town voters were Republicans.
Democrats make up 61% of voters with a college degree. Among voters without a college degree, the split is less significant: 45% voted Democrat and 51% Republican.
It's the economy, stupid

One of the most important factors in this year's midterms is the economy. Prices for gas have increased significantly since the start of the Iran war, and everyday goods have become more and more expensive across the country as well. Almost half of all Americans say their family's financial situation is worse than two years ago.

That sentiment is not the same across the board though. Among those saying their family is better off than two years ago, 75% voted Republican and 23% Democrat. Among those saying they are worse off, only 24% voted Republican and 72% Democrat. President Trump has been saying that the country is on the upswing.
Immigration, economy, the state of democracy: What's the biggest issue for voters?

On the question of which issue facing the country is most crucial, voters are divided among party lines. Of those who said immigration is the most important issue, 89% voted Republican and only 9% voted Democrat. Anti-immigrant rhetoric has been a mainstay of Trump's speeches. He promised to ramp up deportations at the start of his second term. Many states have seen a sharp increase in activity from federal immigration agencies. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) agents have been arresting immigrants off the street, even people who have ongoing asylum application processes, for example. Trump and his supporters say these actions are necessary to make the US safer.

Among those who say that the state of democracy is the most pressing issue in the US, 77% voted Democrat. Congressional Democrats and their supporters have been saying they are concerned about how Trump ignores direct judicial orders, for example to halt deportations, or Congressional resolutions. Among those saying the economy is the most important issue, there's an almost even split of Republican and Democratic voters.
US Iran- and Israel policies

American voters are split on major foreign policy decisions made by the Trump administration. Among those saying that the joint US-Israeli war against Iran was the right decision, 91% were Republican and only 7% Democratic voters. Among those saying it was the wrong decision to attack Iran, 80% were Democratic voters and 16% were Republican voters.

The US support for Israel has been a highly controversial topic ever since Israel began its strikes on Gaza in retaliation to the Hamas terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. The two countries have long been partners, with the US being the most important ally for Israel, and Jewish voters a crucial demographic in the US. But as the humanitarian situation in Gaza deteriorates, support for Israel among the US population, particularly among younger people and liberals, has been wavering. Of those saying US support for Israel is too strong, 77% were Democrat voters and 20% were Republican voters. Among those saying support is about right, only one quarter was Democrat voters.
Domestic policy: dissatisfaction with Congress and country's direction

Looking at how voters felt about the way the majority-Republican Congress did its job over the last two years, there's something of a surprise. Among those dissatisfied with the House's and Senate's work, one third are Republican voters. With the extreme level of polarization in the US, reaching compromises to pass laws or approve a budget in Congress has become harder in recent years. That could be contributing to dissatisfaction.

Of people seeing their country as going in the right direction in general, only 4% were Democrat voters. Of those saying they're dissatisfied or even angry about the US's current direction, 69% were Democrat voters — and 27% Republican, meaning they are unhappy with their own leaders.

Unsurprisingly, 91% of those who said they approved of ICE's actions were Republican, while of those who disapproved, 85% were Democrat. Regarding Trump's tariff policy, there's a split along party lines as well. The president had introduced sharply increased tariffs on goods from a large number of US trading partners. Trump said the move was intended to even out unfair trade balances and protect American manufacturing. He has also used tariffs to punish countries he saw as acting against his political interests. The trade measures have made many goods more expensive for Americans.
Low approval ratings for Trump

Trump is not on the ballot, but the midterms are considered a referendum on how he and his Republicans governed the country for the past two years. Most recently, Trump's approval ratings have fallen to the lowest he has ever had, with just under 30% of Americans saying they think he is doing a good job.
In recent history, only George W. Bush has fared worse, with 25% at the end of his second term. During the 2006 midterm election, Bush's Republican Party lost control of both chambers of Congress.

Exit polls showed that half of voters saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president. Three-quarters of US voters said they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way the country is headed.

According to the AP Voter Poll, dissatisfaction was very high in Democratic-leaning states such as California and Massachusetts. However, even in Republican-leaning states, a majority of voters were at least "dissatisfied."
Can the Democrats flip Congress?

Before Tuesday's election, Republicans (and independents who caucus with them) held 53 of 100 seats in the Senate and 220 of 435 seats in the House. That means they only held two more seats than the 218 required for a majority in the House and only two more than the 51 majority required in the Senate. In recent years, such razor-thin majorities have been the lay of the land, especially in the House of Representatives.
A party doesn’t flip both the House and Senate very often. Since World War II, both chambers have flipped from one party to the other in the same midterm just three times: 1946, 1994 and 2006.

Fact check: Maine interpreters are allowed to help voters, contrary to fraud claims
Claim: "A highly coordinated scheme to steal an election is happening in real time...," a right-wing media outlet said in a X post, viewed more than 600,000 times.
Attached was a CCTV video, showing a man helping people who appear to be Somali-American voters at the polling booth, flipping through papers, marking ballots, and speaking to them as they write.

If the video is authentic, nothing shown in it appears to be illegal. Maine’s election law expressly permits "assistance in reading or marking a ballot" because of a voter's "physical disability, illiteracy, or religious faith."
The Maine Secretary of State’s office told Snopes that the office hasn't received any credible reports of interpreters committing election fraud.

That hasn't stopped users from calling the practice a "blatant violation of state law" or claiming that Somalis were "rigging the election in broad daylight." The Maine Wire — the outlet that shared the video — has been accused in the past of harassing Somali voters at the polls.

articles.title: Aukus is ‘worst, riskiest and most costly’ Australian defence decision ever, public inquiry into submarine deal says
articles.summary:
Report led by Peter Garrett and former defence chief Adm Chris Barrie says agreement should be suspended and calls for royal commission

  • Get our

blocks.text: A public inquiry into the $368bn Aukus nuclear submarine agreement has called the plan “the worst, riskiest and most costly defence decision ever made by an Australian government”, urging its immediate termination.

Former Labor MP and Midnight Oil frontman Peter Garrett and former chief of defence Adm Chris Barrie led the inquiry dominated by critics of the deal with the UK and US, recommending the suspension of plans for new bases and for a royal commission to be held into the agreement signed by the former Morrison government.

Its report, titled Surrendering Australia: the Aukus Deception, says Australia risks being dragged into military conflict with China because of the presence of powerful nuclear submarines. Aukus badly undermines Australia’s sovereignty and undercuts longstanding commitments to nuclear non-proliferation, it says.

The report calls for a rework of the second pillar of the agreement, which covers technology and defence capability sharing, and for a fundamental recalibration of Australia’s relationship with Beijing.

After hearings around the country and more than 1,000 public submissions, the inquiry highlighted a lack of scrutiny and oversight over the five years since Aukus was announced and called for the auditor general and federal parliament to launch independent reviews.
“Since coming to power, Labor has failed to conduct a thorough review of this most significant of defence agreements,” Garrett told the National Press Club in Canberra.
“Conceived in secret, Aukus has spurned established defence and parliamentary oversight practices.”

He said the Stirling defence precinct in Perth risked becoming a “de facto US base” hosting as many as 2,000 serving American personnel, and that nearby communities including Rockingham and Fremantle would become targets for attack.
“The Aukus submarine plan is not tenable,” Barrie, who served as chief of defence between 1998 and 2002, said.
“It’s time for our government to take the lead on this matter. Scrap the Aukus submarine plan now, and rebuild national security decision-making processes.”

Labor agreed to support the deal for Australia to acquire nuclear submarines, which was negotiated under Morrison, then US president Joe Biden and UK prime minister Boris Johnson. As part of the agreement, Australia is funding upgrades to the US defence industrial base and is due to start receiving secondhand Virginia class nuclear submarines around 2032.

blocks.caption: Malcolm Turnbull says faith in Aukus nuclear submarines deal is ‘stark staring bonkers’ – video

blocks.text: But delays and cost blowouts for production of submarines for the US Navy have led to scepticism that Australia will receive the in-service boats.
The UK parliament held a year-long review and, after an inquiry by the Pentagon in 2025, Donald Trump agreed to support Aukus.
after newsletter promotion

But former prime ministers Paul Keating and Malcolm Turnbull, former foreign affairs ministers Gareth Evans and Bob Carr, environmental and security campaigners, and some within Labor believe Aukus is not in Australia’s national interest.
Garrett warned any certainty the US president would eventually agree to send submarines to Australia could not be guaranteed.
“There are no refunds, no enforceable obligations on partner countries, and no recourse if things go wrong,” he said.
The inquiry estimates an additional $180bn will be needed to deal with nuclear waste because of Aukus.

Australia has not identified a permanent storage site for the nuclear waste generated by the submarine fleet, including the high-level radioactive waste from the reactor core and spent fuel, which will remain toxic for thousands of years.
The government’s preferred measure of the total cost of the deal is 0.15% of GDP over its lifetime.

The first Virginia-class nuclear sub from the US is due to arrive in Australia in 2032, with another arriving every four years, before the Australian-built model is ready for operations. The bespoke SSN Aukus model is due to come online in 2042.

articles.title: UBC prof testifies she acted as a 'conduit' for sex assault allegations against Steven Galloway
articles.summary: Anabel Lyon, director of the University of British Columbia's school of creative writing, said she believed the unfounded accusations of a former student who accused bestselling author Steven…

image.caption: Writer Steven Galloway is pictured in his former office at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver on March 31, 2014. He is is suing his accuser and others in a defamation trial. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Anabel Lyon, director of the University of British Columbia's school of creative writing, said she believed the unfounded accusations of a former student who accused bestselling author Steven Galloway of sexual assault.
Annabel Lyon said she was Galloway's colleague when a former grad student accused him of sexual assault
The defamation trial brought by bestselling author Steven Galloway heard testimony Tuesday from the current head of the University of British Columbia's school of creative writing.
Annabel Lyon was called as the defence's first witness and testified she was Galloway's colleague and friend when a former graduate student accused him of sexual assault in November 2015.

Galloway is suing his accuser, known as A.B., claiming she ruined his reputation and career by circulating the unfounded allegations. Three others who also shared the allegations on social media and elsewhere are defendants at the trial.

Lyon testified that she was A.B.'s secondary thesis supervisor or "reader" in 2013 when A.B. submitted an incomplete thesis for graduation. Lyon said when she expressed her concerns to A.B.'s primary adviser, Keith Maillard, she was told A.B. should pass regardless.

"I reached out to Professor Maillard and said, 'I'm not comfortable with this, it's not a complete thesis for our purposes' … He said, 'She really needs to graduate, can you please sign off on it,'" said Lyon.
"I, to this day, regret having done that."

items: Sexual assault claims 'flat out never happened,' ex-UBC professor tells defamation trial
Sex assault allegations diminished performance of Steven Galloway's books: industry expert

blocks.text: Galloway testified earlier that he and A.B., who cannot be named under a publication ban, had a two-year affair while both were married that ended in 2013.
UBC first suspended Galloway in late 2015 citing "serious allegations" and later fired him.
A retired judge hired by UBC to conduct an investigation found that on a balance of probabilities he had not committed sexual assault.
The university later paid Galloway close to $240,000 after two arbitration processes.
Lyon said she believed A.B.'s accusations and spoke to her on the phone about the claims.
Under cross-examination, Lyon said that A.B. asked her to share the accusations, along with an assertion that she would take her story to national media if UBC didn't act against Galloway.

items: Agent of author Steven Galloway says sex assault allegations derailed promising career
'Outrageous' rhetoric alleged in emails as Steven Galloway defamation trial continues

blocks.text: Lyon said she shared what A.B. asked her to at meetings with faculty and other high-level UBC officials. Lyon said she never attempted to verify the information, nor did she feel it was her position to "edit or curate" what A.B. told her.
"I did as [A.B.] asked me to," said Lyon. "I saw myself as a conduit for the information."
Lyon said she also informed UBC administrators of an unsubstantiated report stating that 19 other students had complaints about Galloway.

The report was compiled by former student Chelsea Rooney, who claimed she had been sexually harassed by Galloway. Although she was no longer a student, Rooney acted as investigator, coming up with 19 complaints in a day.
Bestselling author Steven Galloway's defamation trial in 4th week
Lyon said she shared Rooney's report at a meeting in the dean's office "because the university asked me to be that person."
The professor was one of over 20 named defendants when Galloway filed the defamation lawsuit in 2018. She has since come to a confidential out-of-court settlement.
A handful of former defendants, including Rooney, have issued public statements of apology to Galloway.
A.B. is not testifying at the trial, and the court has heard she is not defending the alleged defamatory statements as true.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Karin Larsen is a former Olympian and award-winning sports broadcaster who covers news and sports for CBC Vancouver.

articles.title: Top takeaways from the US midterm elections
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot. They did, and Republicans paid the price on Tuesday, November 3.

blocks.text: OHIO. Supporters celebrate Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton's victory in the midterm elections, at the Democratic Election Night rally, in Columbus, Ohio, US, November 3, 2026.
/Shannon Stapleton/REUTERS
US President Donald Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot. They did, and Republicans paid the price on Tuesday, November 3.

items: Trump's endorsed candidates faced significant defeats, raising questions about his political judgment and the loyalty of his voter base, particularly among key demographics.

Democrats achieved notable victories, including historic wins in traditionally Republican states, suggesting a potential blue wave and a shift in control of Congress, while also placing economic accountability on the party.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
WASHINGTON, USA – Americans went to the polls on Tuesday, November 3, in midterm elections that will determine who controls Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump‘s term.
Here are some early takeaways from the elections.
Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot. They did, and Republicans paid the price on Tuesday.

Early results and exit polls showed an electorate in a sour mood, delivering a strong rebuke of Trump and his agenda as voters expressed deep unhappiness about high prices and the direction of the country.

Many said they feel worse off than two years ago and nearly 9 in 10 identified the cost of living as a crucial or major factor in their vote, according to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets that included major television networks and the Associated Press.

Trump was elected in 2024 on a promise to arrest high inflation, but his tariffs on foreign goods and war against Iran have only worsened the economic situation for many Americans. His response on the campaign trail was to tell Americans to absorb the higher costs even as his popularity sank to record lows.

Nearly two-thirds of voters in the exit polls blamed Trump for high prices, while three-quarters said they were either angry or dissatisfied with the direction of the country. Voters also expressed widespread concern over government corruption.
Early Democratic victories on Tuesday suggested Trump’s 19-state campaign blitz for Republican candidates in recent weeks has done little to improve his standing with voters.

It wasn’t just a bad night for Republicans; it was a bad night for Trump’s judgment. He suffered a series of personal defeats as several candidates he had elevated over the objections of local Republicans struggled in races the party had expected to win.

Trump’s handpicked Senate candidates in South Carolina and North Carolina, Darline Graham and Michael Whatley, lost their races, while Ken Paxton in Texas was struggling against Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. Trump’s choices left Republicans fighting on the defensive in states where they had been favored to win.
The losses are likely to revive questions about Trump’s political instincts, particularly his tendency to prioritize personal loyalty over candidates with broader electoral appeal.
The exit polls showed that the coalition of voters that powered his 2024 victory is badly fractured. Republicans recorded sharp declines in support among Black men, Latinos and young voters.
Opinion polls ahead of the midterms showed a significant chance of a strong Democratic night, with the party favored to reclaim the US House and competing for control of the Senate.
But the scale of the emerging Democratic gains suggested something larger: a potential blue wave that was extending well beyond the traditional battlegrounds.

In flipping the Senate seat in South Carolina, the party made history. Democrats have not won a US Senate race in South Carolina this century and the win by Annie Andrews over Graham became one of the defining upsets of the night.

Democrats were also leading in Kansas, where they last won a Senate seat in 1932, during the Great Depression. In Texas, if Talarico triumphs over Paxton, he would be the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Texas in 38 years.
By 10 pm ET, Democrats were projected by US media outlets to win back control of the US House, and were looking likely to achieve a big majority.
Winning back Congress could be a double-edged sword for Democrats, however.

Voters likely will look to Democrats to address their economic concerns and not just oppose Trump. But they will be limited in what legislation they can pass as the president retains veto power. Trump could also say Democrats are now at the very least equally culpable for the state of the economy. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Tito Sotto seeks clear rules on prolonged unauthorized absences of senators
articles.summary: Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III has filed a resolution seeking to institutionalize guidelines addressing the prolonged unauthorized absence of members of the Senate.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 12:09pm
Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III has filed a resolution seeking to institutionalize guidelines addressing the prolonged unauthorized absence of members of the Senate.
Sotto, chairman of the Senate Committee on Ethics and Privileges, filed Senate Resolution No. 751 on October 27.
Under the resolution, he pointed out a “policy gap” regarding the possible sanction on senators with prolonged unauthorized absences, making them unable to participate in major legislative functions.
“Such absenteeism and neglect of duty is deemed a waste of taxpayer funds and has caused public clamor over the past months,” the resolution read.
Sotto also cited the complaints filed against several senators, whom he did not name in the resolution.

The Senate President Pro Tempore thus underscored the need to revisit the current Rules of the Senate to study “the best possible approach” regarding the matter with the view of ensuring “highest standards of public service commensurate to the trust reposed by the electorate.”

“As public servants elected by the Filipino people and whose salaries and allowances are derived from the taxes they have paid, we owe it to them to perform our duties with diligence and to represent them in the legislative framework,” the resolution added.
He recommended the Committee on Rules to institutionalize the guidelines for such. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Shabu worth P1.36B from Laos seized at Manila port -- PDEA
articles.summary: Authorities seized some 200 kilograms of shabu worth P1.36 billion from a shipment originating from Laos at the Manila International Container Port (MICP) in North Harbor, Manila on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 12:09pm
Authorities seized some 200 kilograms of shabu worth P1.36 billion from a shipment originating from Laos at the Manila International Container Port (MICP) in North Harbor, Manila on Wednesday.
In a statement, the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) said the illegal drugs were found in plastic bags inside cardboard boxes, which were left unclaimed for days.
"The illegal drugs, concealed in 200 vacuum-sealed plastic bags inside 50 cardboard boxes, originated from Laos," PDEA said.
"The seizure comes amid heightened regional efforts against transnational drug trafficking, following the interception of 521 kilograms of shabu in Laos," it added.
This operation was conducted by joint operatives of the PDEA, Bureau of Customs (BOC), and Philippine National Police (PNP).
PDEA said it received intelligence from foreign counterparts in September 2026 regarding a suspected drug shipment bound for the Philippines.
On October 6, the container arrived at Manila North Harbor and underwent X-ray examination, canine inspection, and testing using a Raman spectrometer eight days later.
The tests yielded positive results for shabu.

"After the prescribed period lapsed without anyone claiming the shipment, the cargo underwent abandonment proceedings and was subsequently opened, resulting in the discovery and confiscation of the illegal drugs," PDEA said.
PDEA Director General Undersecretary Isagani Nerez said the seizure shows the importance of intelligence-sharing and coordination with international counterparts.
"This significant seizure demonstrates the importance of intelligence-sharing and close coordination with our international counterparts," Nerez said.

"Following the shabu seizure in Laos, this operation further highlights the need for stronger regional cooperation to prevent drug syndicates from exploiting international shipping routes to bring illegal drugs into our country," he added.
PDEA said backtracking is being conducted to identify the consignee and other individuals behind the shipment.
Those involved may face charges for importation of dangerous drugs under Section 4, Article II of the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
articles.summary:
Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts

The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s…

blocks.text: The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.

The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls show it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.
Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.

Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.

blocks.caption: An ANC poster in Langa township in Cape Town. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters

blocks.text: Johannesburg, Ekurhuleni and Tshwane are in Gauteng, South Africa’s most populous and densely populated province and its economic engine. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance is leading the polls in all three metros but has not been polling above 40%.

The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs with a combination of the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters and the populist Patriotic Alliance and ActionSA across the province’s three metros.

blocks.caption: Helen Zille is campaigning to become mayor of Johannesburg. Photograph: Kim Ludbrook/EPA

blocks.text: In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to controversial past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.

The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.

blocks.caption: Jacob Zuma addresses an election rally in KwaMashu, north of Durban, on Sunday. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma is polling above 40%. The 84-year-old Zuma, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.
The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.

South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

articles.title: Prosecutors asks ICC to admit testimonies detailing police’s ‘modus operandi’
articles.summary: In a motion filed under Rule 68(3) of the ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Office of the Prosecutor requested authorization to introduce the prior recorded statements, interview transcripts,…

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 11:57am

MANILA, Philippines — Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court have asked Trial Chamber III to admit written witness testimonies alleging systemic police tactics and fabricated accounts during the war on drugs of detained former President Rodrigo Duterte.

In a motion filed under Rule 68(3) of the ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Office of the Prosecutor requested authorization to introduce the prior recorded statements, interview transcripts, and associated case materials of four key witnesses into the official court record.
The submission focuses on establishing the operational patterns of the Philippine National Police (PNP) during drug operations.

According to court documents, the witness statements provide detailed accounts of police officers allegedly planting firearms and methamphetamine, locally known as “shabu," near victims' bodies to simulate self-defense scenarios, commonly framed in official reports as “nanlaban” incidents.

The documents filed by the prosecution further outline how official PNP reports were routinely fabricated and submitted internally as positive "accomplishments," alongside the deployment of paid police assets and financial incentives for officers involved in extrajudicial executions.

Trial Chamber III is scheduled to open the trial proper on November 30, where the former chief executive faces three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder during his tenure as Davao City Mayor and as president of the Philippines.
The prosecution has also asked the court to admit testimonies of other witnesses, which are expected to be 60 to 70, according to the prosecution.
RELATED: Duterte ICC trial: Prosecutors seek to admit three witness accounts
Testimonies
The prosecution's motion centers on the written testimonies of four key witnesses, each providing critical evidence regarding different operational facets of Duterte’s drug war.
Witness P-1136
Witness P-1136 indicated that Duterte targeted public officials as "high-value targets" who were allegedly involved in the illegal drug trade.
He also stated that these targeted individuals were often recorded on the presidential drug watchlist, known as the “PRRD List.”

Furthermore, the prosecution highlighted that Witness P-1136 provided evidence going toward proof of Duterte's policy to "neutralize" local public officials allegedly involved with illegal drugs, as well as his public threats directed against high-value targets.

“P-1136 was [REDACTED]. In his statement, P-1136 indicates that Mr Duterte targeted public officials as “high-value targets” (“HVT”) allegedly involved in the illegal drug trade,a nd often recorded in the PRRD List,” the prosecution said.
Witness P-1345
According to the prosecution, witness P-1345 detailed specific patterns in police modus operandi during anti-illegal drug operations in Manila, particularly under "One Time Big Time" drives.
The witness indicated that police officers routinely planted shabu and firearms near victims' bodies to simulate self-defense scenarios and justify the killings.

Additionally, Witness P-1345 provided evidence regarding the practice of "red-tagging," noting that administration critics, labor leaders, and members of the judiciary were systematically labeled as drug personalities or subversives.

“P-1345 describes: (i) the structure and functioning [REDACTED]; (ii) the establishment of an Extrajudicial Killing (“EJK”) [REDACTED] due to an escalation in the killings;19 and (iii) the lack of cooperation from the PNP during [REDACTED]. P-1345’s statement includes detailed discussions of nine case files [REDACTED] of PNP killings of alleged drug personalities during the “war on drugs”. P-1345 identifies patterns in the modus operandi of PNP killings, including planting shabu and guns near the victim’s body. P-1345 also explains that journalists, human rights groups, labour leaders and judges who opposed Mr Duterte’s administration were ‘red-tagged’ as drug personalities or communists.”
Witness P-1391
Witness P-1391 also detailed institutional patterns within police operations, stating that official PNP reports were routinely fabricated following anti-drug operations.
The witness indicated that police deployed paid assets to carry out executions and offered monetary incentives to officers for carrying out killings.
Additionally, Witness P-1391 provided direct evidence regarding specific charged events, including Incidents 21 and 30, which involved the aftermath of the killing of 17-year-old Kian delos Santos.

“P-1391’s evidence further assists with the proof of Incidents 21 and 30. As such, the Four Witnesses’ evidence goes to the proof of the contextual elements of crimes against humanity and to the policy to ‘neutralise’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines,” the prosecution said.
Witness P-1404

According to the prosecution's filing, witness P-1404 detailed community-level surveillance mechanisms, stating that local barangay clearance policies and inter-agency efforts were used to systematically track individuals on drug watchlists.

The witness indicated that local officials were directed through the Department of the Interior and Local Government to submit updated drug watchlists on a monthly basis and to utilize community monitoring programs like “MASA MASID.”
Additionally, Witness P-1404 highlighted internal police reporting practices, noting that police officers routinely recorded and presented extrajudicial killings as official accomplishments.

“P-1404 also provides evidence on: barangay clearance policy; the different types of watchlist (including PDEA, barangay, PNP, [REDACTED] Department of Interior and Local Government (“DILG”) and Presidential); how the Co-Perpetrators ordered barangay captains via the DILG to submit updated watchlists each month; and the MASA MASID programme.He speaks about the process [REDACTED]. [REDACTED]. He also [REDACTED] and evidences reporting and the presentation of killings as “accomplishments”. P-1404’s Prior Recorded Testimony goes to proof of a policy to ‘neutralise’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines. It also provides evidence of barangay clearance policy, including [REDACTED].”

articles.title: Weapon or wine bottle? China disputes reports of artillery shell in Papua New Guinea
articles.summary: Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the 32kg object was "merely a dummy".

blocks.text: Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle".
"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing skeptical comments.
Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city.
Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery".

In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this.
Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said.
However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea.
"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally".
Some Facebook users appear unconvinced.
"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them.
Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

articles.title: C5 rehabilitation to start in late November, target completion by early 2028
articles.summary: The P2.5 billion rehabilitation of Circumferential Road 5 (C5) will begint this November and is projected to end in early 2028

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 11:21am
Circumferential Road 5 (C5) passes through various cities in Metro Manila, including business district Makati City.
Canva / Mel Casipit
MANILA, Philippines — Rehabilitation of Circumferential Road 5 (C5) begins this November, with construction set to finish by early 2028, according to the Department of Public Works and Highways.

The 23-kilometer C5 road rehabilitation project from Kalayaan Interchange to Commonwealth Avenue is set to begin in the last week of November, Public Works Secretary Giovanni Lopez confirmed in an interview on Tuesday, November 3.

Based on the project's scope work, the rehabilitation will include base correction and asphalt overlay to improve the safety of the major thoroughfare. The project will also include widened sidewalks for pedestrians and cyclists, Lopez said.

It will take "more or less around 420 calendar days," Lopez said. If construction starts on time by late November, the project will be completed by February or the last week of January 2028, the DPWH chief added.
The northbound section of the C5 Boni Serrano Flyover was closed over Undas weekend for asphalt patching, lane marking, repainting of fences and installation of additional road delineators.
Structural strengthening work is also underway at the Pasig Boulevard-C5 Flyover in Barangay Bagong Ilog.
C5 covers various cities in Metro Manila, with pathways leading to central business districts like Ortigas Center, Bonifacio Global City and Makati City.

Construction work will take place from 10 p.m. to 4 a.m. to prevent disrupting the flow of traffic, as was done during the first phase of the Epifanio de los Santos Avenue (EDSA) rehabilitation project.
Rehabilitation of C5 is valued at P2.5 billion and is funded by unused funds from the initial P17-billion budget for EDSA.
